paras: The lynching of Jim Nelson was the hanging of a Black farm laborer of about 19 by twenty or thirty mounted men on the road about three miles from Jefferson, Chesterfield County, South Carolina, on Saturday night, November 21, 1903. Nelson had been accused of attempting to assault the young daughter of his employer and was taken from two men who were carrying him to the sheriff. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of "parties unknown," and South Carolina papers noted that it was the county's first lynching.

On the afternoon of November 15, according to the reports, Nelson, a laborer on the farm of Miles W. Porter, was accused of an attempt to "outrage" Porter's 7-year-old daughter at a spring near the house. The children ran to the house and gave the alarm; the papers said the attempt was not accomplished. Nelson fled, and a posse searched the woods and swamps for several days without finding him.

The girl's father and brothers kept up the hunt, and on Saturday afternoon Will Porter came upon Nelson at Maynard's sawmill near Catarrh. He held him in the Jefferson guard house, and that evening Porter and E. G. Ingram set out by buggy to deliver him to the sheriff at Chesterfield.

About three miles from Jefferson two men came out of the woods with revolvers and ordered the buggy up the road to a tree, 200 yards on in the Chesterfield account and 100 in the Columbia dispatch. There Nelson was dragged from the buggy, and Ingram and Porter were ordered to turn around and drive off. Some twenty or thirty horsemen waiting there hanged him from the limb with a rope and rode away.
The State's correspondent, who said he visited the scene, wrote that none of the party appeared drunk and no shot was fired; a family 200 yards away learned what had happened only the next morning.

Nelson's body was left hanging through Sunday, and hundreds of people came to look at it. On Sunday evening the coroner empanelled a jury at the scene and held the inquest by the light of pine knots; the verdict was that Nelson "had met his death at the violent hands of parties unknown to the jury." The body was buried near the road, no relatives having come to claim it.

At Chesterfield, the correspondent reported, the news "was received here very quietly and elicited little comment on the streets." No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial was found in the coverage.

Nearly all coverage descended from a special report to The State from Chesterfield and a Columbia dispatch, both of November 23. The Savannah Morning News ran the Columbia version on its front page on November 24 under the headline "Life the Penalty: A Negro Brute Paid to Lynchers for His Attempt Upon a Little White Girl," adding that Chesterfield County "had its first lynching." The story called the lynchers "knights of the cord" and the act "the illegal hanging"; the Atlanta Constitution printed it on November 30 as "Black Lynched for Attempt."

The Lancaster Ledger, the Newberry Herald and News and the Sumter Watchman and Southron reprinted The State's special under "The Usual Crime the Cause," with its blackjack limb that "hung invitingly over the road" and lynchers who showed no "swearing or boisterous conduct." The Bamberg Herald printed a shorter version, and in December the Lexington Dispatch and the Anderson Intelligencer gave it a sentence or two, the latter saying Nelson was "quietly lynched" for "attempting the usual crime."

Elsewhere it ran as a one-line wire brief, first in the Topeka State Journal on November 24 and then in weekly digests, several of which placed Jefferson in North Carolina. No account of the lynching was found in the Black press.

A version printed by the Brunswick Daily News on November 25 named the victim John Nelson and said that after being hanged he was "riddled with bullets." The on-scene correspondent's account and the Columbia dispatch say instead that not a shot was fired, and they and the inquest verdict name him Jim Nelson.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Nelson
bases: Twenty or thirty mounted men took Nelson from two men carrying him to the sheriff and hanged him from a tree, which the papers call 'the illegal hanging' (A1, A4, A7).

Nelson was hanged by 'twenty or thirty men on horseback' after being taken from his captors on the way to the sheriff (A1, A4, A7); the papers call it an 'illegal hanging' and tie it to the accusation of an attempted assault on a white child (A1, A2, A11).

Thirteen papers carried the lynching, but every detailed version (A1, A3, A4, A6, A7) traces to one report for The State by a correspondent who visited the scene, and the briefs (A2, A9, A11, A12) condense it; no independent account was found.

accounts.label: The State's correspondent (Chesterfield special)
accounts.gist: A correspondent who said he visited the scene described the stop by two armed men, the 20 or 30 horsemen, the hanging from a blackjack limb 200 yards up the road, and an orderly, sober, silent mob; not a shot fired.

accounts.label: Columbia dispatch (Nov. 23)
accounts.gist: The same account sent from Columbia, with the inquest verdict of 'parties unknown' and burial by the road; it puts the limb about 100 yards up the road and the departure at about 8 o'clock.

accounts.label: Brunswick version (Columbia, Nov. 24)
accounts.gist: Names the victim John Nelson and says a posse formed when word of the capture spread, met the two men on the road, and swung Nelson to a tree and 'riddled' him 'with bullets'.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Found that Nelson died 'at the violent hands of parties unknown to the jury'.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'A Negro Brute Paid to Lynchers for His Attempt Upon a Little White Girl' and called the mob 'knights of the cord', while also calling the act 'the illegal hanging'.

The State's special, reprinted in Lancaster, Newberry and Sumter, headed it 'The Usual Crime the Cause' and wrote of a limb that 'hung invitingly over the road' and of lynchers who were not drunk and did not swear.
South Carolina state-news columns gave a sentence or two: 'lynched and hanged by a mob' (Lexington), 'quietly lynched' for 'the usual crime' (Anderson).
Northern papers ran a one-line wire brief, several placing Jefferson in North Carolina.

versions.value: Nelson was 'riddled with bullets' after being hanged

conflicts.note: The no-shots version comes from the correspondent who visited the scene and is repeated in the Columbia dispatch; the Brunswick version's final sentence departs from that text.
Only the Brunswick version uses 'John'; the inquest verdict as reported names 'Jim Nelson'.
The on-scene State special gives 200 yards.
The N. C. form appears only in one-line northern briefs; every South Carolina-datelined account says Chesterfield County, S. C.
A publication matter; all detailed accounts put the lynching on Saturday night.

sources.note: Columbia, Nov. 23 dispatch, full version: accusation, capture, seizure from buggy by 20-30 horsemen, body hung all Sunday, coroner's inquest 'parties unknown', burial by the road; 'Not a shot was fired'.
quotes: Chesterfield county has heretofore been clear of lynching, and the illegal hanging Saturday night is the second execution to occur within her borders in almost a half century.
A NEGRO BRUTE PAID TO LYNCHERS FOR HIS ATTEMPT
The verdict was that Jim Nelson had met his death at the violent hands of parties unknown to the jury.
A rope was placed around his neck, and he was swung up and left hanging, while the knights of the cord rode silently away into the darkness.
